stories.nickname: The afternoon I did eleven conversations
stories.situation: Rundweg had seven weeks of runway, a bridge round that had verbally committed and then did not sign, and eleven people. Jonas was the co-founder who ran operations and payroll and was the one who could see the cash position daily.
stories.stakes: Eight of the eleven had been there more than two years. Two had moved cities for the job. German insolvency law meant that if he kept trading past the point of knowing, he would be personally liable.
actions: Told his two co-founders the number three weeks before either of them wanted to accept it, and made them look at the weekly cash sheet with him
Filed for insolvency on the day it became legally required rather than the week after, which cost them the small chance the bridge would revive
Did all eleven conversations himself in one afternoon, which he now thinks was wrong
Wrote references for all eleven and made calls for nine of them
Paid the two who had relocated an extra month from his own savings, about 7,000 euros, which the administrator later queried
stories.result: The company ceased trading in June 2026. Nine of the eleven were in new jobs within three months. Creditors were paid at about 40 cents in the euro. He has not been pursued personally.
stories.reflection: He should have taken two days over the conversations rather than one afternoon; doing them in a block was for him, not for them, and he knows that because three people told him so afterwards. He also should have shown the cash sheet to his co-founders monthly from the start instead of carrying it alone.

stories.nickname: The per-drop price I set too low
stories.situation: Rundweg charged per drop. Jonas set the price in 2023 from the cost of a Berlin drop, and the model worked there. Through 2024 the company grew into Leipzig and Dresden, where drop density was about a third of Berlin's, and the same price lost money on every delivery.
stories.stakes: The two new cities were 44% of volume by the end of 2024 and the blended margin had gone from positive to about minus 11% without anyone changing a number.
actions: Built a per-city unit model in a weekend once he suspected it, which the company had never had
Took it to the board with the conclusion that two-thirds of their growth was destroying value
Argued for raising prices in the two cities and losing volume, against his co-founder who wanted to keep growth for the next round
Raised prices in Leipzig in February 2025 as a test and lost 38% of the volume there
stories.result: The Leipzig test showed the price could not rise enough to work at that density. They exited Dresden in April 2025 and the blended margin returned to about plus 4%. The exit also halved the growth rate, which is a significant part of why the bridge round did not sign.
stories.reflection: The model should have existed from the first month; he built the business on a single city's economics and called it a unit model when it was an average. He also notes, without resolving it, that being right about the price is what killed the round.

stories.nickname: The riders who asked for a contract
stories.situation: Rundweg's 34 riders were freelancers, as every competitor's were. Six of them asked for employment contracts, and under German law they had a reasonable case that they were employees in all but name.
stories.stakes: Converting them would raise the cost per drop by about 22% and the company was nine months from needing a round. Fighting it was the standard play in the sector and would probably have worked for two years.
actions: Got a legal opinion that said the riders were likely right, and showed it to the board rather than burying it
Converted all 34 rather than the six who asked, over four months
Rebuilt the route planning to absorb some of the cost, which recovered about 9 of the 22 percentage points
Told investors before they asked, in the quarterly update rather than in a meeting
stories.result: All 34 were employed by October 2025. Cost per drop rose about 13% net of the route changes. Rider attrition fell from 61% a year to 19%, which he had not predicted and which made the service more reliable. Two investors called it a mistake.
stories.reflection: He is still certain it was right and still aware it shortened the runway that ran out. He does not have a version of this story where both things are not true.

stories.nickname: The five months I did not work
stories.situation: After the shutdown Jonas did not work for five months. He had savings for three and borrowed from his brother for the other two. He was not interviewing; he was sleeping badly and had stopped answering messages from two of the eleven.
stories.stakes: It is the gap on his record, and the thing he has least worked out how to describe.
actions: Saw a therapist from the second month, which his brother arranged
Wrote up what happened at Rundweg as a forty-page document for himself, which is where the unit model post-mortem came from
Answered the two messages in month four
Took the first consulting client in September because a former customer asked, not because he had been looking
stories.result: He has two clients and bills enough. The forty pages are the reason he can describe the pricing mistake precisely. He is in touch with nine of the eleven.
stories.reflection: He thought the five months were wasted and now does not. He is clear that he would not have been useful in a job in July, and equally clear that 'I needed time' is not a thing he can say to a recruiter, which is the part he is still working out.

stories.nickname: The night shift I worked for a month
stories.situation: At Nordlicht, Jonas was the analyst whose model said the night shift was 18% less productive. The night supervisor said the model was wrong. Jonas asked to work the shift for a month to find out.
stories.stakes: Nothing, except that his manager thought it was a waste of an analyst's time and said so.
actions: Worked nineteen night shifts as a picker
Found the model counted a trailer as available when it was on site, not when it was unloaded, and nights waited an average of 40 minutes a trailer
Rewrote the measure rather than the shift's targets
Gave the finding to the night supervisor to present, not himself
stories.result: The productivity gap closed to 3% once measured properly. The night supervisor presented it and was promoted the following year. Jonas was made team lead four months later.
stories.reflection: He learned that the data was describing a measurement, not the world, which is a mistake he then made again at Rundweg with the unit model. He is aware of the symmetry and does not like it.

goals.shortTerm: An operating role at a logistics or commerce company with real scale — a regional general manager or a head of operations for a business unit — in Germany or the Netherlands, where the unit economics are someone's actual job.
goals.longTerm: To run a logistics business he did not found, at a size where the decisions are about capital allocation rather than survival. He is specific that he does not intend to found another company in the next ten years.
goals.planB: Continue consulting and take a general manager role at a smaller operator, which is available to him now and which he thinks would teach him less.
goals.whyMba: He has run a company and still cannot read a balance sheet the way his investors could. He never had a mentor, never worked under anyone who had done it before, and every lesson cost eleven people their jobs. He wants the next set of lessons to be cheaper.
goals.whyNow: The shutdown is recent enough to be the thing he has learned the most from and far enough behind him that he can describe it. Waiting two years would turn it into an anecdote.
